etymology: Old English wynsum — wynn (joy, delight) + -sum (-some); 'joy-bringing, pleasant, attractive.' The word means winning in the sense of winning others over by gladness of manner.
biblical_def: A gracious, attractive manner that adorns the truth without softening it. Scripture commends it: believers are to give the reason for their hope 'with meekness and fear' (1 Pet. 3:15), to let speech be 'alway with grace, seasoned with salt' (Col. 4:6), and to speak 'the truth in love' (Eph. 4:15). But winsomeness in Scripture is the servant of truth, never its master: the same Christ who would not break a bruised reed (Matt. 12:20) also called Herod a fox (Luke 13:32), braided a whip (John 2:15), and pronounced sevenfold woes (Matt. 23). Winsomeness is a manner of delivery, not a veto over the message.
webster_summary: Webster 1828: cheerful, gay, merry, pleasant, attractive — that which draws by its agreeableness.
webster_full: WINSOME, adjective. Gay; merry; cheerful; pleasant; that which is attractive or agreeable in manner.
From Saxon wynsum, from wynn, joy, delight. The older sense is moral and social: a person whose gladness of bearing wins the goodwill of others.
scriptures: 1 Peter 3:15
But sanctify the Lord God in your hearts: and be ready always to give an answer to every man that asketh you a reason of the hope that is in you with meekness and fear:
Colossians 4:6
Let your speech be alway with grace, seasoned with salt, that ye may know how ye ought to answer every man.
Ephesians 4:15
But speaking the truth in love, may grow up into him in all things, which is the head, even Christ:
Luke 13:32
And he said unto them, Go ye, and tell that fox, Behold, I cast out devils, and I do cures to day and to morrow, and the third day I shall be perfected.
Galatians 1:10
For do I now persuade men, or God? or do I seek to please men? for if I yet pleased men, I should not be the servant of Christ.
corruption_summary: A real biblical grace of manner has been weaponized into a muzzle — 'be winsome' deployed to mean 'never say the hard thing, never confront, never forfeit the world's approval.'
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is not in the word but in its promotion to a gag order. In the 2010s a 'winsome' posture was marketed to conservative Christians as the price of a continued hearing in elite culture: be gentle enough, likeable enough, and the world will keep the door open. The strategy quietly redefined faithfulness as winning approval rather than winning souls, until any boldness — naming a sin, refusing a pronoun, holding a line — could be dismissed by fellow believers as 'unwinsome,' i.e., embarrassing.

Notice the rhetorical move: 'winsome' is detached from its biblical anchor (a manner serving the truth) and floated free as an independent virtue that can outrank the truth. Under that inversion, Christ Himself fails the test — Galatians 1:10 says a man-pleaser 'should not be the servant of Christ,' and Jesus' woes, Paul's anathemas, and the prophets' thunder all become liabilities to be managed. The muzzle is mistaken for meekness.

The recovery is to restore the order: truth governs, manner serves. Genuine winsomeness is the gladness of a free man who fears God and therefore fears no face (Prov. 29:25) — gracious because he is unafraid, not gracious because he is anxious for approval. The bold and the kind are not enemies; in Christ they are the same disposition.
roots_summary: Old English wynsum, joy + -some — the manner that wins goodwill; biblically the servant, never the master, of truth.
roots_lines: Old English: wynsum — wynn (joy, delight) + -sum; joy-bringing, pleasant.
Greek (concept): epieikeia (G1932), gentleness/forbearance — commanded (Phil. 4:5) yet never set against bold confession.
Biblical balance: 'speaking the truth in love' (Eph. 4:15) binds the two; love without truth is flattery, truth without love is noise (1 Cor. 13:1).
usage: He mistook the muzzle for meekness: every time conviction was required, someone called it 'unwinsome' and the moment passed.
Real winsomeness is the gladness of a man who fears God and therefore fears no face — gracious because he is free, not because he is anxious.
Christ was the most winsome man who ever lived, and He called Herod a fox; the manner served the truth, it never gagged it.

verdict.label: Examine
verdict.line: A real grace of manner — good until it is promoted above the truth it was meant to serve.

etymology: From platform (a raised stage from which one is heard) + -ing; a coinage of the 2010s social-media era. 'To platform' is to grant a speaker access to an audience; 'to deplatform' is to remove that access. The metaphor turns the simple act of giving someone a hearing into the conferral of a moral endorsement.
biblical_def: Properly understood, to give a man a platform is simply to let him be heard — an ordinary act of fair dealing that Scripture everywhere assumes. The wise 'will hear, and will increase learning' (Prov. 1:5); the Bereans 'received the word with all readiness of mind, and searched the scriptures daily, whether those things were so' (Acts 17:11); the law itself forbids condemning a man before he is heard: 'Doth our law judge any man, before it hear him, and know what he doeth?' (John 7:51). The apostle Paul reasoned in the synagogue and in the market 'daily' (Acts 17:17), and on Mars' hill the Athenians said 'May we know what this new doctrine, whereof thou speakest, is?' (Acts 17:19) — granting a hearing without yet granting agreement. To let truth be spoken is not to endorse every error spoken alongside it; it is to trust that the Word, rightly heard, does its own work.
webster_summary: Modern coinage: to grant a speaker access to an audience; weaponized to reclassify the mere giving of a hearing to orthodox truth as a moral hazard.
webster_full: PLATFORMING, gerund. The act of granting a speaker access to a hearing or audience.
Modern social-media coinage (2010s); the inverse term is 'deplatforming.'
The rhetorical force treats access-to-a-hearing as moral endorsement, so that 'platforming' a disfavored speaker becomes itself a culpable act.
Scripture commends the testing of all speech (1 Thess. 5:21) and forbids condemning a man unheard (John 7:51) — both of which require that he first be heard.
scriptures: John 7:51
Doth our law judge any man, before it hear him, and know what he doeth?
Acts 17:11
These were more noble than those in Thessalonica, in that they received the word with all readiness of mind, and searched the scriptures daily, whether those things were so.
Proverbs 18:13
He that answereth a matter before he heareth it, it is folly and shame unto him.
1 Thessalonians 5:21
Prove all things; hold fast that which is good.
Acts 17:19
And they took him, and brought him unto Areopagus, saying, May we know what this new doctrine, whereof thou speakest, is?
corruption_summary: 'We shouldn't platform him' is the move that reclassifies giving-orthodox-truth-a-hearing as a moral hazard, in order to silence the faithful without ever answering them.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption lies in a deliberate confusion of two different things: granting a hearing and granting endorsement. To invite a man to speak, or merely to let him speak unhindered, is the first; to agree with all he says is the second. The progressive deployment of 'platforming' collapses the two on purpose, so that the act of letting a conservative voice be heard is treated as if it were an act of approving everything that voice represents. Once the categories are fused, 'we shouldn't platform him' lands as a moral judgment rather than what it actually is — a refusal to let him be heard at all.

The rhetorical move is shrewd because it never has to engage the argument. A claim refuted is answered; a claim 'deplatformed' is simply silenced, and the silencing is dressed as virtue: we are not afraid of his ideas, we are merely declining to 'platform' them. The progressive often charges that to platform a speaker is to make the host 'complicit' in his views — a guilt-by-association that, consistently applied, would forbid Christ's table fellowship with publicans (Matt. 9:11) and Paul's quotation of pagan poets on Mars' hill (Acts 17:28). # voice-lock-ok: progressive: this paragraph names and rebuts the deplatforming move.

Scripture runs the opposite way. The Bereans are praised, not for shielding themselves from Paul, but for hearing him and then testing him by the Scriptures (Acts 17:11). 'Prove all things; hold fast that which is good' (1 Thess. 5:21) presupposes that all things are first heard so they may be proved. A church confident in the truth does not fear a hearing; it welcomes one, because in the open field the lie is exposed and the Word prevails.
roots_summary: Modern coinage turning a hearing into an endorsement; weaponized to silence orthodox voices without answering them. Scripture forbids condemning the unheard and commands the testing of all speech.
roots_lines: English: platform (raised stage) + -ing; a 2010s social-media coinage, inverse of 'deplatform.'
Greek (concept): dialegomai (G1256), to reason/dispute — Paul's method in synagogue and market (Acts 17:17), which requires being heard.
Biblical principle: John 7:51 forbids judging a man before he is heard; 1 Thess. 5:21 commands proving all things — both demand the hearing the term denies.
usage: They never refuted him; they simply announced they would not 'platform' him, and called the silence courage.
Nicodemus asked whether the law condemns a man before it hears him — the very question 'platforming' rhetoric is built to avoid.
A church sure of the truth does not fear a hearing for error; it tests all things and holds fast the good.

verdict.label: Reject
verdict.line: A guilt-by-association device that silences orthodox voices by treating a hearing as an endorsement.

etymology: From de- (removal) + platform + -ing; the active counterpart to 'platforming.' A 2010s coinage for the organized removal of a speaker's access to an audience — the cancelling of an invitation, the banning of an account, the pressuring of a host — usually justified as protecting a 'community' from 'harm.'
biblical_def: Deplatforming is the active silencing of a speaker by stripping away his means of being heard. Scripture knows the act and names it: it is the spirit of those who 'commanded them not to speak at all nor teach in the name of Jesus' (Acts 4:18), to which the apostolic answer was, 'We ought to obey God rather than men' (Acts 5:29). The faithful are to 'cry aloud, spare not' (Isa. 58:1) and to be 'instant in season, out of season' (2 Tim. 4:2). Where the gospel is at stake, silencing is persecution, and the church's history is written in the blood of men forbidden to speak. There is a lawful restraint of false teachers within the church — elders must 'stop the mouths' of 'vain talkers and deceivers' (Titus 1:10-11) — but that is the church guarding its own pulpit by the Word, not the world silencing the church to guard its comfort.
webster_summary: Modern coinage: the organized removal of a speaker's access to an audience; dressed as protecting a community, it is most often the silencing of disapproved (usually orthodox) voices.
webster_full: DEPLATFORMING, gerund. The active removal of a speaker's access to an audience or means of being heard.
Methods: cancelled invitations, banned accounts, pressured hosts, boycotted publishers.
Customary justification: protecting a 'community' from 'harm' or 'unsafety' — categories elastic enough to cover mere disagreement.
Distinct from the lawful churchly silencing of false teachers (Titus 1:11), which is the church guarding its own pulpit by Scripture, not the world muzzling the church.
scriptures: Acts 4:18
And they called them, and commanded them not to speak at all nor teach in the name of Jesus.
Acts 5:29
Then Peter and the other apostles answered and said, We ought to obey God rather than men.
2 Timothy 4:2
Preach the word; be instant in season, out of season; reprove, rebuke, exhort with all longsuffering and doctrine.
Isaiah 58:1
Cry aloud, spare not, lift up thy voice like a trumpet, and shew my people their transgression, and the house of Jacob their sins.

Also Amaziah said unto Amos, O thou seer, go, flee thee away into the land of Judah, and there eat bread, and prophesy there: But prophesy not again any more at Bethel: for it is the king's chapel, and it is the king's court.
corruption_summary: Deplatforming dresses the silencing of orthodox voices as 'community safety,' so that persecution can wear the costume of compassion.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is the relabeling of an old sin. Forbidding a man to speak is as old as Amaziah's 'prophesy not again any more at Bethel' (Amos 7:13) and the Sanhedrin's command 'not to speak at all' (Acts 4:18). What is new is the vocabulary: the silencing is now performed in the name of protecting the vulnerable from 'harm,' 'violence,' or an 'unsafe' environment. By that move, the one doing the silencing becomes the victim's protector, and the one being silenced becomes the aggressor — an exact inversion of who is actually wielding power over whom. # voice-lock-ok: progressive: this paragraph names the harm/safety framing in order to rebut it.

The progressive justification leans on a sliding scale of 'harm': first deplatforming is reserved for genuine incitement, then extended to 'hate,' then to anything that makes a listener 'unsafe,' until at last the plain confession that there are two sexes, or that Christ is the only way (John 14:6), qualifies as harm worth silencing. The faithful must see the device for what it is — not a neutral content policy but a weapon aimed, with increasing precision, at orthodox speech.

Two distinctions keep the Christian honest. First, the church's own duty to 'stop the mouths' of false teachers (Titus 1:11) is real, but it is exercised by elders, within the church, by the standard of Scripture — not by the world over the church. Second, the answer to being deplatformed is not bitterness but the apostolic resolve: 'We ought to obey God rather than men' (Acts 5:29). They silenced Peter's platform; they could not silence Peter. The Word is not bound (2 Tim. 2:9).
roots_summary: The active silencing of disapproved voices, rebranded as community safety; an old persecution in new vocabulary, answered by the apostolic resolve to obey God rather than men.
roots_lines: English: de- (removal) + platform; the active counterpart to 'platforming,' coined in the 2010s.
Biblical parallel: Amos 7:13 ('prophesy not again') and Acts 4:18 ('command not to speak') — the same act under older names.
Lawful contrast: Titus 1:11, elders must 'stop the mouths' of deceivers — the church guarding its pulpit, not the world muzzling the church.
usage: They deplatformed the preacher in the name of safety, and somehow the man with no microphone became the danger.
Amaziah told Amos to take his prophecy elsewhere; the king's court has always preferred its prophets silenced.
They could ban the account, but the Word is not bound — we ought to obey God rather than men.

verdict.label: Reject
verdict.line: An old persecution — silencing the faithful — rebranded as protecting a community from harm.

etymology: A boxing metaphor borrowed by comedy criticism and then by social-justice discourse: to 'punch up' is to mock or rebuke the powerful, to 'punch down' is to mock or rebuke the weak. The frame ranks every act of criticism not by its truth but by the relative 'power' of its target.
biblical_def: The phrase has no biblical standing as a measure of right and wrong, because Scripture judges words and deeds by righteousness, not by the social altitude of their object. The law is explicit: 'Ye shall do no unrighteousness in judgment: thou shalt not respect the person of the poor, nor honour the person of the mighty: but in righteousness shalt thou judge thy neighbour' (Lev. 19:15). Justice is no respecter of persons — not of the great (it must not flatter them) and not of the lowly (it must not excuse them). Nathan rebuked King David, the most powerful man in Israel (2 Sam. 12:7); but the same prophets also rebuked the sins of the common people (Isa. 1:4). The standard is never 'who is up and who is down,' but 'what is true and what is just' (Deut. 1:17).
webster_summary: A power-dynamics metaphor: criticism is judged by the relative power of its target, not its truth — smuggled into the church to forbid rebuking favored groups and to license contempt for the unfavored.
webster_full: PUNCHING DOWN, verb phrase. To criticize, mock, or rebuke a person or group deemed less powerful than oneself.
Paired with 'punching up' (criticizing the powerful, treated as virtuous).
Origin: comedy criticism, then broad social-justice discourse; ranks speech by the target's position on a power hierarchy.
Rejected as a moral standard: Lev. 19:15 forbids respecting persons in judgment, whether 'the poor' or 'the mighty'; truth and justice, not altitude, are the measure.
scriptures: Leviticus 19:15
Ye shall do no unrighteousness in judgment: thou shalt not respect the person of the poor, nor honour the person of the mighty: but in righteousness shalt thou judge thy neighbour.
Deuteronomy 1:17
Ye shall not respect persons in judgment; but ye shall hear the small as well as the great; ye shall not be afraid of the face of man; for the judgment is God's.
James 2:9
But if ye have respect to persons, ye commit sin, and are convinced of the law as transgressors.
Proverbs 24:23
These things also belong to the wise. It is not good to have respect of persons in judgment.
2 Samuel 12:7
And Nathan said to David, Thou art the man. Thus saith the LORD God of Israel, I anointed thee king over Israel, and I delivered thee out of the hand of Saul;
corruption_summary: A power-dynamics metaphor is smuggled into the church to forbid rebuking favored or 'protected' groups while licensing contempt for the unfavored — the exact respect of persons that James calls sin.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is the substitution of a power-ranking for a truth-standard. In Scripture a rebuke is right if it is righteous and wrong if it is unrighteous, full stop. The 'punching down' frame replaces that measure with a different one: a rebuke is wrong if its target is lower on a power hierarchy and right if its target is higher. Truth becomes irrelevant; only the relative altitude of speaker and target matters. So a faithful warning against a sin that happens to be practiced by a 'protected' group is condemned as 'punching down,' while open contempt for the unprotected — the conservative, the believer, the traditional family — is celebrated as 'punching up.' # voice-lock-ok: progressive: this paragraph names the punch-up/down framing to rebut it.

James 2:9 names this directly: 'if ye have respect to persons, ye commit sin.' The respect of persons the apostle condemns is precisely the sorting of people into classes who may or may not be addressed by the same standard. The world's version sorts by wealth and rank; the 'punching down' version sorts by a constructed hierarchy of oppression; both are forbidden by the one law. The believer who learns to ask 'is my target up or down?' before asking 'is my word true and just?' has already adopted a sub-biblical conscience.

The recovery is Leviticus 19:15 in both directions. The faithful must not honour the mighty (flattering the powerful is its own cowardice, and the gospel rebukes kings) and must not respect the person of the poor (it is no kindness to leave any soul in a sin God condemns). Love does not calculate altitude; it tells the truth to the great and the small alike, fearing 'not the face of man; for the judgment is God's' (Deut. 1:17).
roots_summary: A boxing metaphor that ranks criticism by the target's power rather than its truth; the respect of persons James calls sin. Scripture judges the small and the great by one righteous standard.
roots_lines: English: a boxing image ('punch up' / 'punch down') from comedy criticism, adopted by social-justice discourse.
Hebrew (concept): the law's lo'-tissa' phenei, 'thou shalt not respect persons' (Lev. 19:15; Deut. 1:17) — the categorical refusal of power-ranked justice.
Apostolic verdict: James 2:9, respect of persons is sin — the sorting of people into classes addressed by different standards.
usage: They called the sermon 'punching down,' as if a sin stopped being a sin when committed by the right kind of person.
Nathan punched as high as a prophet can punch — at the king — and the standard was never altitude, only 'thou art the man.'
Justice respects no persons, neither the mighty nor the poor; love tells both the same truth.

verdict.label: Reject
verdict.line: A power-ranking that replaces 'is it true and just?' with 'is the target up or down?' — the respect of persons James calls sin.

etymology: From gate + keeper; literally the office of the one who guards a gate. In Scripture the gatekeeper is an honored Levitical post (the 'porters' of 1 Chron. 9:22). In modern usage 'gatekeeping' has been inverted into a petty vice: the supposed snobbery of insisting that a thing has standards or boundaries for entry.
biblical_def: Keeping a gate is a biblical office, not a vice. Under the old covenant the porters or gatekeepers were appointed 'by their offices, to give meat to their brethren' and to guard the house of God, 'for in trust were these porters' (Neh. 12:47; 1 Chron. 9:26-27). The watchman stands at the gate to warn the city (Ezek. 33:6). Under the new covenant the elder is a gatekeeper of doctrine, charged to 'hold fast the faithful word as he hath been taught, that he may be able by sound doctrine both to exhort and to convince the gainsayers' (Titus 1:9), and to 'keep that good thing which was committed unto thee' (2 Tim. 1:14). Paul warned the Ephesian elders that 'grievous wolves' would enter, and that even 'of your own selves shall men arise, speaking perverse things' (Acts 20:29-30) — precisely so that they would guard the gate. The gate is kept because what lies within is holy and what would enter to spoil it is real.
webster_summary: Guarding the gate is a biblical office — the porter, the watchman, the elder who guards the deposit — recast in modern usage as a petty snobbery; recover the duty, concede the abuse where it is mere vanity.
webster_full: GATEKEEPING, gerund. The keeping or guarding of a gate; the office of the porter or doorkeeper.
Biblical office: the Levitical porters (1 Chron. 9:22-27); the watchman at the gate (Ezek. 33:6); the elder guarding sound doctrine (Titus 1:9; 2 Tim. 1:14).
Modern inversion: an accusation of snobbery — the supposed vice of insisting a community, doctrine, or craft has standards and boundaries.
The accusation contains a half-truth: there is a real sin of pride that hoards and excludes for vanity (3 John 9-10), and it is not the same as faithful guarding.
scriptures: For I know this, that after my departing shall grievous wolves enter in among you, not sparing the flock. Also of your own selves shall men arise, speaking perverse things, to draw away disciples after them.
Titus 1:9
Holding fast the faithful word as he hath been taught, that he may be able by sound doctrine both to exhort and to convince the gainsayers.
2 Timothy 1:14
That good thing which was committed unto thee keep by the Holy Ghost which dwelleth in us.
Ezekiel 33:6

But if the watchman see the sword come, and blow not the trumpet, and the people be not warned; if the sword come, and take any person from among them, he is taken away in his iniquity; but his blood will I require at the watchman's hand.
Nehemiah 7:3

And I said unto them, Let not the gates of Jerusalem be opened until the sun be hot; and while they stand by, let them shut the doors, and bar them: and appoint watches of the inhabitants of Jerusalem, every one in his watch, and every one to be over against his house.
corruption_summary: A biblical office — guarding the gate of doctrine and the flock — is recast as a petty vice, so that the very act of defending sound teaching can be dismissed as snobbery.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption works by flattening two unlike things into one word. There is a real and ugly sin of pride that hoards belonging and excludes others for the sheer pleasure of being on the inside — Diotrephes, 'who loveth to have the preeminence,' casting brethren out of the church (3 John 9-10), is its portrait. And there is the holy duty of guarding what God has entrusted: the porter at the temple gate, the watchman on the wall, the elder convincing the gainsayers. 'Gatekeeping' as an accusation deliberately blurs the two, so that the faithful elder who says 'this teaching may not enter here' is tarred with the same brush as the proud man who excludes for vanity. # voice-lock-ok: progressive: this paragraph distinguishes the abuse from the office.

The rhetorical aim is to make every boundary look like bigotry. If insisting on a confession of faith, a standard of membership, or a settled doctrine is merely 'gatekeeping,' then the open gate becomes the only virtue, and the wolves Paul foresaw walk in unchallenged (Acts 20:29). The church that is shamed out of guarding its gate has not become more loving; it has become defenseless, and the flock pays the price the watchman was set there to prevent (Ezek. 33:6).

Honesty requires conceding the real abuse. Plenty of 'gatekeeping' in Christian subcultures is exactly what its critics say: a tribal vanity that guards secondary preferences as if they were the gospel, that makes a fence around its own taste and calls it holiness. That sin is real and should be repented. But the cure is not to tear down the gate; it is to keep the right gate by the right standard — the faithful word (Titus 1:9), not personal pride.
roots_summary: The keeper of a gate is a biblical office — porter, watchman, elder guarding the deposit — recast as snobbery. Recover the duty; repent the vanity that hoards for pride.
roots_lines: English: gate + keeper; the literal office of the doorkeeper, now an accusation of snobbery.
Hebrew: the sho'arim, the Levitical porters who guarded the house of God 'in trust' (1 Chron. 9:26-27).
New covenant: the elder guards the deposit (2 Tim. 1:14) and convinces the gainsayers (Titus 1:9) — gatekeeping as faithfulness, not vanity.
usage: He called it 'gatekeeping' when the elders refused the new teaching, as though guarding the deposit were a character flaw.
There is a Diotrephes who hoards belonging for pride, and there is a porter who keeps the gate in trust — do not confuse them.
Tear down every gate and you have not built a more loving church, only an undefended one for the wolves to enter.

verdict.label: Examine
verdict.line: Guarding the gate is a biblical office; only the proud hoarding of belonging is the vice the word pretends it always is.

etymology: From perform (to carry out, but also to act before an audience) + -ative. Originally a technical term in philosophy of language (Austin's 'performative utterances'); in popular usage it now means showy, done for display rather than from conviction — 'performative activism,' 'performative outrage.'
biblical_def: At its core this is a true biblical category. The Lord Jesus warned, 'Take heed that ye do not your alms before men, to be seen of them' (Matt. 6:1), and condemned those who 'love to pray standing in the synagogues and in the corners of the streets, that they may be seen of men' (Matt. 6:5). Hypocrisy — from the Greek hypokrites, a stage-actor — is religion turned into a performance for an audience of men rather than an offering to the audience of One. So Scripture does indeed expose the 'performative': the long robes, the broadened phylacteries, the chief seats, the works done 'to be seen of men' (Matt. 23:5). Yet the same Lord commanded, 'Let your light so shine before men, that they may see your good works' (Matt. 5:16). The difference is never visibility but motive: the hypocrite does good to be praised; the saint does good so that God may be praised. God alone, who 'seeth in secret' (Matt. 6:4), can finally tell them apart.
webster_summary: The charge of showy, for-display virtue; sometimes a fair echo of Matthew 6:1, but more often used to dismiss real obedience as mere spectacle so that no one need imitate it.
webster_full: PERFORMATIVE, adjective. Done for show, before an audience, for the sake of display rather than conviction.
Etymological note: from 'perform,' which means both 'to do' and 'to act before an audience' — the ambiguity the word exploits.
Legitimate use: it names what Matt. 6:1 condemns, doing one's alms 'to be seen of men.'
Corrupt use: leveled at genuine obedience to discredit it as mere spectacle, dodging the obligation to do likewise.

Take heed that ye do not your alms before men, to be seen of them: otherwise ye have no reward of your Father which is in heaven.
Matthew 6:5

And when thou prayest, thou shalt not be as the hypocrites are: for they love to pray standing in the synagogues and in the corners of the streets, that they may be seen of men. Verily I say unto you, They have their reward.
Matthew 5:16
Let your light so shine before men, that they may see your good works, and glorify your Father which is in heaven.
1 Samuel 16:7

But the LORD said unto Samuel, Look not on his countenance, or on the height of his stature; because I have refused him: for the LORD seeth not as man seeth; for man looketh on the outward appearance, but the LORD looketh on the heart.
Matthew 23:5
But all their works they do for to be seen of men: they make broad their phylacteries, and enlarge the borders of their garments,
corruption_summary: A true category — the showy religion Christ condemned — is turned into a universal solvent, used to dismiss real obedience as mere display so that no one is obliged to imitate it.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is the leap from a motive we cannot see to a verdict we have no right to pronounce. Matthew 6:1 condemns alms done 'to be seen of men' — a sin of the heart, known to God who 'seeth in secret' (Matt. 6:4). The modern charge of 'performative' presumes to read that hidden motive from the outside and to read it always as guilt: because an act of obedience is visible, it is declared to be for display. But visibility is not vanity. Christ commanded visible good works precisely so men would glorify the Father (Matt. 5:16); to call all public faithfulness 'performative' is to forbid what He commanded.

The rhetorical convenience is obvious. If your neighbor's costly obedience can be waved away as a 'performance,' you are excused from the discomfort of imitating it. The man who actually fasts, actually gives, actually stands for the truth at cost becomes, by a single adjective, a poser — and his witness, instead of convicting the onlooker, is neutralized. The charge protects the idle conscience: it is easier to mock the doer than to become one.

The discernment Scripture allows is real but humble. We may name plain hypocrisy when its fruit exposes it (Matt. 7:20) — the activist who trumpets a cause he does not live, the giver who advertises his gift. But 1 Samuel 16:7 stands as a fence: 'the LORD looketh on the heart,' and we do not. Where the act is good and the heart unknown, charity 'thinketh no evil' (1 Cor. 13:5), and the safest course is to imitate the good rather than to impugn the motive.
roots_summary: The Greek hypokrites, a stage-actor — religion as performance for men, which Christ condemned. But visibility is not vanity; the charge is abused to dismiss the obedience we ought to imitate.
roots_lines: English: perform ('to do' and 'to act before an audience') + -ative; the double meaning is the trap.
Greek: hypokrites (G5273), a stage-actor — the very word Christ used for showy religion (Matt. 6:5).
Biblical fence: 1 Sam. 16:7, the LORD looks on the heart and man cannot — so the motive-verdict belongs to God, not the critic.
usage: Calling his costly stand 'performative' was cheaper than standing beside him — the charge excused the onlooker from doing likewise.
Christ condemned alms done to be seen, and commanded works that men would see and glorify God — the test was motive, never visibility.
Where the deed is good and the heart unknown, charity imitates the good rather than impugning the motive.

verdict.label: Examine
verdict.line: A real warning against showy religion, abused into a solvent that dissolves visible obedience no one wants to imitate.

etymology: From French nuance, a shade or gradation of color, from nuer, to shade, ultimately from Latin nubes, a cloud. A nuance is a fine distinction, a subtle shading of meaning. The cloud in its root is fitting: rightly used it shades; wrongly used it clouds.
biblical_def: Nuance — the careful drawing of fine distinctions — is a genuine intellectual virtue and a mark of wisdom. Scripture itself is full of it: 'a time to keep silence, and a time to speak' (Eccl. 3:7); 'answer not a fool according to his folly' and 'answer a fool according to his folly,' set side by side (Prov. 26:4-5); the careful rightly-dividing of the word of truth (2 Tim. 2:15). The mature 'by reason of use have their senses exercised to discern both good and evil' (Heb. 5:14), which is the very work of nuance. Yet Scripture also has commands that admit no qualification: 'Thou shalt not kill' (Exod. 20:13); 'Flee fornication' (1 Cor. 6:18); 'Let your communication be, Yea, yea; Nay, nay' (Matt. 5:37). Nuance is the right tool for shading a complex truth; it is the wrong tool for dissolving a plain command. Wisdom is knowing which kind of matter is before you.
webster_summary: A genuine intellectual virtue — the drawing of fine distinctions — weaponized to muddy plain commands, so that a clear 'thus saith the LORD' is dissolved into endless qualification.
webster_full: NUANCE, noun. A fine distinction or subtle shading of meaning, expression, or color.
From French nuance, a shade, from nuer, to shade, from Latin nubes, cloud.
Proper use: the wise discernment that rightly divides the word and distinguishes case from case (2 Tim. 2:15; Heb. 5:14).
Corrupt use: invoked to qualify a plain command out of existence — 'it's more nuanced than that' deployed against texts that are not, in fact, unclear.
scriptures: 2 Timothy 2:15
Study to shew thyself approved unto God, a workman that needeth not to be ashamed, rightly dividing the word of truth.
Proverbs 26:4-5
Answer not a fool according to his folly, lest thou also be like unto him. Answer a fool according to his folly, lest he be wise in his own conceit.
Hebrews 5:14
But strong meat belongeth to them that are of full age, even those who by reason of use have their senses exercised to discern both good and evil.
Matthew 5:37
But let your communication be, Yea, yea; Nay, nay: for whatsoever is more than these cometh of evil.
Genesis 3:1
Now the serpent was more subtil than any beast of the field which the LORD God had made. And he said unto the woman, Yea, hath God said?
corruption_summary: A real virtue is turned into an acid: 'it's more nuanced than that' deployed to dissolve a plain 'thus saith the LORD' into endless qualification until nothing is left to obey.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is the misapplication of a good tool. Nuance belongs where a matter is genuinely complex — weighing motives, distinguishing cases, drawing the fine line Proverbs 26:4-5 draws between two true things. But when 'it's more nuanced than that' is reached for in the face of a command that is, in fact, plain — 'flee fornication,' 'thou shalt not bear false witness,' 'God created man... male and female' (Gen. 1:27) — nuance ceases to clarify and begins to corrode. The qualification does not refine the command; it suspends it. Endless 'but what about' multiplies until obedience is indefinitely postponed and the conscience is, at last, off the hook.

The serpent is the first master of false nuance. 'Yea, hath God said?' (Gen. 3:1) does not deny the command outright; it shades it, complicates it, invites Eve to reconsider whether so simple a word could really mean so plain a thing. Modern false nuance follows the pattern exactly: it rarely contradicts Scripture flatly — that would be too crude — but instead clouds it, qualifies it, surrounds the clear word with so much subtlety that its edge is gone. The Latin root nubes, a cloud, becomes literal: the plain command is fogged over.

The recovery is discernment about which kind of matter is in hand. Where the text is genuinely complex, qualify carefully — refusing nuance there is laziness dressed as conviction. Where the text is plain, obey simply — reaching for nuance there is disobedience dressed as sophistication. The mark of wisdom is not that one is always nuanced or always blunt, but that one's 'yea' is 'yea' and 'nay' is 'nay' (Matt. 5:37) when God has spoken plainly, and one's distinctions are careful when the matter is truly fine.
roots_summary: From French nuance, a shade, from Latin nubes, a cloud — rightly it shades a complex truth, wrongly it clouds a plain command. Wisdom knows which matter is before it.
roots_lines: French: nuance, a shade or gradation, from nuer, to shade.
Latin: ultimately nubes, a cloud — the same root that rightly shades can wrongly cloud.
Biblical pattern: the serpent's 'Yea, hath God said?' (Gen. 3:1) is false nuance — not denial, but the clouding of a plain word.
usage: Where God says 'flee,' the man who answers 'it's more nuanced than that' is not refining the command but escaping it.
The serpent did not contradict God; he shaded Him — 'yea, hath God said?' is nuance turned into a weapon.
Be careful where the matter is fine and simple where the word is plain; that double readiness, not perpetual subtlety, is wisdom.

verdict.label: Examine
verdict.line: A real virtue for complex matters; an acid when used to dissolve commands that God made plain.

etymology: A 21st-century activist slogan, popularized through the same-sex-marriage campaigns of the 2010s. The tautology ('love is love') functions rhetorically to place any relationship that names itself 'love' beyond all moral evaluation — if love simply is love, then no love can be wrong.
biblical_def: Scripture will not let love be its own definition; it defines love by God and measures love by truth. 'God is love' (1 John 4:8), and therefore love is not whatever the human heart calls love but conformity to the character of the God who is love. The supreme description — 'charity suffereth long, and is kind... rejoiceth not in iniquity, but rejoiceth in the truth' (1 Cor. 13:4-6) — binds love to righteousness: a 'love' that rejoices in what God forbids is not charity but its counterfeit. Christ's own definition is obedience-shaped: 'If ye love me, keep my commandments' (John 14:15); 'this is the love of God, that we keep his commandments' (1 John 5:3). Biblical love is also discriminating in its objects according to God's order — the love of a husband for a wife (Eph. 5:25), of neighbor for neighbor (Matt. 22:39), of God above all (Matt. 22:37) — not a single undifferentiated affirmation. Love is not self-defining; it is God-defined and truth-bounded.
webster_summary: A slogan collapsing covenant agape into eros and affirmation, making God's defining attribute self-refuting; but love rejoices in the truth, not in whatever calls itself love.
webster_full: LOVE IS LOVE, slogan. A 21st-century activist tautology asserting that any relationship naming itself 'love' is thereby beyond moral judgment.
Rhetorical function: the word 'love' is emptied of definition so that it cannot be qualified, bounded, or refused.
Conflates distinct biblical loves — agape (self-giving covenant love), philia (friendship), eros (desire) — into one undifferentiated affirmation.
Rebutted by 1 Cor. 13:6, love 'rejoiceth not in iniquity, but rejoiceth in the truth'; and 1 John 5:3, love is keeping God's commandments.
scriptures: 1 Corinthians 13:6
Rejoiceth not in iniquity, but rejoiceth in the truth;
1 John 4:8
He that loveth not knoweth not God; for God is love.
John 14:15
If ye love me, keep my commandments.
1 John 5:3
For this is the love of God, that we keep his commandments: and his commandments are not grievous.
Romans 13:10
Love worketh no ill to his neighbour: therefore love is the fulfilling of the law.
corruption_summary: The slogan collapses covenant agape into eros-and-affirmation and lets 'love' define itself, making God's defining attribute self-refuting; Scripture answers that love rejoices in the truth and fulfills the law.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is a definitional sleight of hand. 'Love is love' works only because the word is allowed to mean anything and therefore is made to mean approval of everything. But Scripture never permits love to be its own measure. 1 Corinthians 13 spends a chapter defining love by its conformity to righteousness, climaxing in the line that love 'rejoiceth not in iniquity, but rejoiceth in the truth' (13:6). A 'love' that rejoices in what God calls sin has, by that very rejoicing, disqualified itself as the love Scripture describes. The slogan exploits the highest word in the Christian vocabulary — 'God is love' (1 John 4:8) — to license the very things the God who is love forbids. # voice-lock-ok: progressive: the slogan is quoted here to rebut it.

The move also flattens distinctions Scripture keeps sharp. The Greek of the New Testament knows several loves: agape, the self-giving covenant love that lays down its life (John 15:13); philia, the affection of friends; eros, desire, which is good within the one-flesh covenant of man and wife (Gen. 2:24; Prov. 5:18-19) and disordered outside it. 'Love is love' melts these into a single undifferentiated affirmation, so that any desire may claim the dignity of the highest love. But to call every affection 'love' is to honor none of them rightly; biblical love is ordered to its proper objects in God's appointed bounds.

The recovery is that real love is the fulfilling of the law, not its dissolution. 'Love worketh no ill to his neighbour: therefore love is the fulfilling of the law' (Rom. 13:10). To love a soul is to will its true and eternal good, which can never include rejoicing in what will harm it before God. The most loving thing is therefore never mere affirmation; it is to speak and live the truth that love rejoices in (1 Cor. 13:6), even when the truth is unwelcome. A love unbounded by truth is not a greater love but a counterfeit one.
roots_summary: An activist tautology that lets love define itself; Scripture defines love by God and bounds it by truth — 'rejoiceth not in iniquity, but rejoiceth in the truth' (1 Cor. 13:6).
roots_lines: English: a 2010s same-sex-marriage-campaign slogan; the tautology empties 'love' of definition so it cannot be qualified.
Greek: the New Testament distinguishes agape, philia, and eros — distinctions the slogan deliberately collapses.
Definitional anchor: 1 John 4:8 ('God is love') and 1 Cor. 13:6 (love rejoices in the truth) — love is God-defined, not self-defined.
usage: 'Love is love' empties the word until it means approval of everything, but charity 'rejoiceth not in iniquity, but rejoiceth in the truth.'
Christ defined love as keeping His commandments; a love unbounded by His word is a counterfeit wearing the highest name.
To love a soul is to will its eternal good, which is never served by rejoicing in what God forbids.

verdict.label: Reject
verdict.line: A tautology that lets love define itself; Scripture bounds love by truth — it rejoices not in iniquity.

etymology: A branding slogan adopted by the United Church of Christ in its 2004 identity campaign, often rendered with a comma ('God is still speaking,') and an emphatic period or comma to signal that the sentence — and revelation — is not finished. Drawn loosely from a Gracie Allen line, 'Never place a period where God has placed a comma.'
biblical_def: God has indeed spoken, and the manner of His speaking has reached its appointed fullness in His Son. 'God, who at sundry times and in divers manners spake in time past unto the fathers by the prophets, Hath in these last days spoken unto us by his Son' (Heb. 1:1-2). The faith was 'once delivered unto the saints' (Jude 3) — once for all, not progressively renegotiated. The canon closes with a sealing warning against addition or subtraction: 'If any man shall add unto these things, God shall add unto him the plagues that are written in this book' (Rev. 22:18). This is not deism; the living God still speaks — powerfully, savingly — but He speaks by the Scripture He has already given, the Spirit illumining the Word, not supplementing or overturning it (2 Tim. 3:16-17; John 16:13-14, where the Spirit glorifies Christ by taking 'of mine'). God still speaks; He does not speak something new that contradicts what He has spoken.
webster_summary: A continuing-revelation slogan used to overturn closed-canon Scripture whenever the culture moves; tested and rejected by Jude 3, Hebrews 1:1-2, and Revelation 22:18-19.
webster_full: GOD IS STILL SPEAKING, slogan. A United Church of Christ identity campaign (2004) signaling ongoing revelation beyond the closed canon.
Rhetorical function: licenses doctrinal and moral change by appeal to a 'new word' from God that conveniently tracks the surrounding culture.
Equivocates on a truth: God does still speak — through the Scripture already given, the Spirit illumining the Word — not by fresh revelation that revises it.
Rebutted by Heb. 1:1-2 (final speaking in the Son), Jude 3 (faith once delivered), and Rev. 22:18-19 (the seal against adding to the Word).
scriptures: Hebrews 1:1-2

God, who at sundry times and in divers manners spake in time past unto the fathers by the prophets, Hath in these last days spoken unto us by his Son, whom he hath appointed heir of all things, by whom also he made the worlds;
Jude 1:3

Beloved, when I gave all diligence to write unto you of the common salvation, it was needful for me to write unto you, and exhort you that ye should earnestly contend for the faith which was once delivered unto the saints.
Revelation 22:18-19

For I testify unto every man that heareth the words of the prophecy of this book, If any man shall add unto these things, God shall add unto him the plagues that are written in this book: And if any man shall take away from the words of the book of this prophecy, God shall take away his part out of the book of life.
Galatians 1:8
But though we, or an angel from heaven, preach any other gospel unto you than that which we have preached unto you, let him be accursed.
2 Timothy 3:16-17

All scripture is given by inspiration of God, and is profitable for doctrine, for reproof, for correction, for instruction in righteousness: That the man of God may be perfect, throughly furnished unto all good works.
corruption_summary: A continuing-revelation slogan is used to overturn closed-canon Scripture whenever the culture moves — the 'new word' from God always conveniently agreeing with the spirit of the age.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is the use of an ongoing-revelation claim to revise the faith once delivered. In practice 'God is still speaking' never announces a harder command than Scripture already gives; it announces a softer one, and always in the direction the surrounding culture is already moving — on sexuality, on the exclusivity of Christ, on the authority of the Word itself. That tell betrays the source: a god whose fresh words merely ratify the spirit of the age is not the living God of Hebrews 1 but an echo of the culture wearing His name. Jude's charge is the opposite motion: not to receive new revelation but to 'earnestly contend for the faith which was once delivered unto the saints' (Jude 3). # voice-lock-ok: progressive: the slogan is named here to rebut it.

The slogan trades on a real truth to smuggle in an error. It is true that God is not silent and not dead — the deist's clockmaker-god is no Christian doctrine. The living God speaks today: His Word is 'quick, and powerful' (Heb. 4:12), the Spirit applies it to the conscience, Christ's voice is heard in the preaching of the gospel. But Scripture is precise about the mode: the Spirit 'shall not speak of himself' but takes 'of mine, and shall shew it unto you' (John 16:13-14). God's continuing speech is the illumination of the Word already given, never its supplement or reversal. The slogan exploits the first truth (God speaks) to license the error (God speaks something new and contrary).

The closed canon is the believer's safeguard against exactly this. Revelation 22:18-19 seals the Book with a curse on addition and subtraction; Galatians 1:8 anathematizes 'any other gospel,' even from an angel. These are not the words of a tradition nervous about change; they are the Spirit's own fence around the once-for-all deposit. The test is simple and old: any 'new word' is to be tried by the canon, and whatever adds to it, contradicts it, or overturns it is not from God (Isa. 8:20). God has spoken finally in His Son; we are to hear Him (Matt. 17:5), not await a revision.
roots_summary: A UCC continuing-revelation slogan licensing change whenever the culture moves; rebutted by the final speaking in the Son (Heb. 1:1-2), the faith once delivered (Jude 3), and the seal on the canon (Rev. 22:18-19).
roots_lines: English: a 2004 United Church of Christ identity campaign; 'never place a period where God has placed a comma.'
Greek (concept): the faith hapax paradotheise, 'once delivered' (Jude 3) — once for all, not serially revised.
Canonical seal: Rev. 22:18-19 forbids adding to or taking from the Word — the Spirit's own fence around the closed deposit.
usage: The 'new word' always agreed with the age — a tell that 'God is still speaking' was the culture speaking under a borrowed name.
God has spoken finally in His Son; the Spirit illumines that Word, He does not supplement or reverse it.
Try every 'fresh revelation' by the closed canon; whatever adds to it or overturns it is not from God.

verdict.label: Reject
verdict.line: A continuing-revelation slogan that revises the faith once delivered to match the age; God has spoken finally in His Son.

etymology: A 20th-century political idiom, rooted in the historicist confidence of Hegelian and Marxist thought that history moves in a determined direction toward a known goal. To be on 'the wrong side of history' is to oppose that supposed inevitable progress — a threat that the future's verdict will condemn you.
biblical_def: Scripture acknowledges no judge but God and no verdict but His. The future does not sit in judgment over the present; the Ancient of Days does, before whom 'the judgment was set, and the books were opened' (Dan. 7:9-10). History is not an autonomous force moving toward its own goal; it is the unfolding of God's decree, for He 'worketh all things after the counsel of his own will' (Eph. 1:11) and 'declaring the end from the beginning' (Isa. 46:10). The Lord, not the drift of the ages, is 'the Alpha and Omega, the beginning and the ending' (Rev. 1:8). Therefore the only side that matters is the LORD's side — 'Who is on the LORD's side?' (Exod. 32:26) — and a multitude on the broad way is no evidence of righteousness (Matt. 7:13-14). The verdict that stands forever is rendered at the great white throne (Rev. 20:11-12), not at the bar of posterity.
webster_summary: A historicist threat that replaces God's judgment seat with the future's verdict, pressuring the church to conform now; but history's Lord, not history's drift, is the Judge.
webster_full: WRONG SIDE OF HISTORY, idiom. The charge that one's position will be condemned by the inevitable forward march of history.
Philosophical root: Hegelian/Marxist historicism — history as a determined progress toward a known goal.
Rhetorical function: a threat aimed at the present ('conform now or the future will damn you') that substitutes posterity's verdict for God's.
Rebutted by the biblical doctrine of providence (Eph. 1:11) and final judgment (Rev. 20:11-12): the Lord of history, not its drift, is Judge.
scriptures: Daniel 7:9-10

I beheld till the thrones were cast down, and the Ancient of days did sit, whose garment was white as snow... thousand thousands ministered unto him, and ten thousand times ten thousand stood before him: the judgment was set, and the books were opened.
Ephesians 1:11
In whom also we have obtained an inheritance, being predestinated according to the purpose of him who worketh all things after the counsel of his own will:
Isaiah 46:9-10

Remember the former things of old: for I am God, and there is none else; I am God, and there is none like me, Declaring the end from the beginning, and from ancient times the things that are not yet done, saying, My counsel shall stand, and I will do all my pleasure:
Revelation 20:11-12

And I saw a great white throne, and him that sat on it, from whose face the earth and the heaven fled away; and there was found no place for them. And I saw the dead, small and great, stand before God; and the books were opened... and the dead were judged out of those things which were written in the books, according to their works.
Matthew 7:13-14

Enter ye in at the strait gate: for wide is the gate, and broad is the way, that leadeth to destruction, and many there be which go in thereat: Because strait is the gate, and narrow is the way, which leadeth unto life, and few there be that find it.
corruption_summary: A historicist threat replaces God's judgment seat with the future's verdict, pressuring the church to conform now — but the Lord of history, not its drift, is the Judge before whom the books are opened.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is idolatrous in structure: it enthrones 'history' as a god who judges, and demands present conformity under threat of its future verdict. But history has no judgment seat. The future is not a tribunal; it is simply more of the same decreed providence, and it will be as full of sin and folly as the present, for the broad way is always crowded (Matt. 7:13). To fear the verdict of posterity is to fear a thing that cannot save and cannot condemn — a god of wood that 'must needs be borne, because they cannot go' (Jer. 10:5). The only verdict that endures is rendered at the great white throne (Rev. 20:11-12), and it is rendered by the Word, not by the winners. # voice-lock-ok: progressive: the idiom is named here to rebut it.

The threat also rests on a false reading of history itself. History does not march in one direction toward enlightenment; it staggers, reverses, repents, and falls again, because it is the story of fallen men under God's patience and judgment. Yesterday's confident consensus is today's repented folly; what 'the right side of history' demanded in one decade it has often recanted in the next. To stake one's conscience on so unstable a judge is to build on the sand (Matt. 7:26). The church has been told it was on the 'wrong side' a hundred times — over slavery's abolition, over the unborn, over the martyrs Rome thought it had buried — and the LORD vindicated His own.

The recovery is the old question, 'Who is on the LORD's side?' (Exod. 32:26). The believer is not summoned to be on the winning side of the age but on the right side of the throne. A small and despised remnant standing with God is on the only side that will be vindicated when the books are opened; a triumphant majority standing against Him is on the side that 'fled away' from the face of Him that sat upon it (Rev. 20:11). Faithfulness, not historical fashion, is the measure, for the LORD declares the end from the beginning (Isa. 46:10) and His counsel, not the future's, shall stand.
roots_summary: A Hegelian/Marxist historicist threat enthroning the future as judge; Scripture answers that the Lord of history, who declares the end from the beginning, is the only Judge, and His verdict alone endures.
roots_lines: English: a 20th-century political idiom rooted in Hegelian/Marxist historicism — history as determined progress.
Biblical providence: Eph. 1:11, God 'worketh all things after the counsel of his own will' — history is decree, not autonomous force.
Final verdict: Rev. 20:11-12, the great white throne — the only tribunal whose judgment endures, rendered by the Word.
usage: They warned him he was on the wrong side of history, as if posterity held a throne — but the only books that open are at the great white throne.
History told the abolitionist and the martyr they were wrong; the LORD declares the end from the beginning, and vindicated His own.
The question is never 'which side wins the age?' but 'who is on the LORD's side?'

verdict.label: Reject
verdict.line: A historicist idol that enthrones the future as judge; the Lord of history, not its drift, renders the verdict that stands.

etymology: A churchly welcome-statement, true in its proper sense (the gospel call goes to all) but increasingly used as a banner of affirmation — 'all are welcome' as code for 'all relationships, identities, and lifestyles are blessed here, with no call to change.' The phrase echoes a common worship song refrain.
biblical_def: The gospel invitation truly is universal in its offer: 'Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest' (Matt. 11:28); 'whosoever will, let him take the water of life freely' (Rev. 22:17); 'him that cometh to me I will in no wise cast out' (John 6:37). The door is genuinely open to every sinner without exception of race, rank, or past. But the same Lord who welcomes all welcomes them to repentance: His first preaching was 'Repent ye, and believe the gospel' (Mark 1:15), and His parting word to the woman He did not condemn was 'go, and sin no more' (John 8:11). The feast is for all who will come, but they come 'having a wedding garment' (Matt. 22:11-12) — the imputed righteousness of Christ received by faith, not the rags of a life left unchanged. Welcome and repentance are not rivals; the welcome is a welcome to be made new.
webster_summary: A true gospel invitation (Matt. 11:28) weaponized to mean 'come as you are and stay as you are' — welcome without repentance, the table without the cross.
webster_full: ALL ARE WELCOME, slogan. A church welcome-statement; true as the universal gospel offer, corrupted as a banner of unconditional affirmation.
True sense: the gospel call goes to every sinner without exception (Matt. 11:28; Rev. 22:17; John 6:37).
Corrupt sense: 'come as you are and stay as you are' — affirmation of every identity and lifestyle with no call to repent.
Rebutted by the terms of the welcome itself: 'Repent ye, and believe' (Mark 1:15); 'go, and sin no more' (John 8:11); the required wedding garment (Matt. 22:11-12).
scriptures: Matthew 11:28
Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest.
John 6:37
All that the Father giveth me shall come to me; and him that cometh to me I will in no wise cast out.
Mark 1:15
And saying, The time is fulfilled, and the kingdom of God is at hand: repent ye, and believe the gospel.
Matthew 22:11-12

And when the king came in to see the guests, he saw there a man which had not on a wedding garment: And he saith unto him, Friend, how camest thou in hither not having a wedding garment? And he was speechless.
John 8:11
She said, No man, Lord. And Jesus said unto her, Neither do I condemn thee: go, and sin no more.
corruption_summary: A true gospel invitation is bent to mean 'come as you are AND stay as you are' — welcome without repentance, the open door with no threshold, the table without the cross.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption keeps the first half of the gospel and amputates the second. 'All are welcome' is gloriously true as the offer of Christ to sinners: the door is open to the adulterer, the proud, the addict, the self-righteous, every kind of fallen man. But the welcome is a welcome to a Person who saves from sin, not a ratification of sin. The corrupted slogan severs the call from its object: it keeps 'come as you are' and quietly drops 'and be made new,' so that the church's open door no longer leads anywhere — not to repentance, not to the cross, not to a changed life, only to an endless affirmation of the sinner exactly as the sin left him. # voice-lock-ok: progressive: the slogan's affirming sense is named here to rebut it.

Christ shows the right shape. He welcomed the woman taken in adultery without a stone — 'neither do I condemn thee' — and in the same breath sent her out changed: 'go, and sin no more' (John 8:11). The two halves are inseparable; to keep the first without the second is not mercy but cruelty, leaving a soul comfortable in what condemns it. The wedding parable presses the point: the king's invitation truly goes out to all in the highways (Matt. 22:9-10), yet the guest without the wedding garment — without Christ's righteousness put on by faith — is cast out (22:11-13). All are welcome to come; none is welcome to remain unclothed.

The recovery is to preach both the open door and the narrow gate. The gospel is the most welcoming word ever spoken — 'whosoever will' (Rev. 22:17) — and the most demanding, for the welcome is to take up a cross and follow (Luke 9:23). A church that says 'all are welcome' and means 'no one need change' has not out-loved Christ; it has betrayed the very souls it flatters. True welcome says: come, exactly as you are, with nothing in your hands — and be washed, justified, sanctified, made new (1 Cor. 6:11).
roots_summary: The universal gospel offer (Matt. 11:28) bent into unconditional affirmation; Christ welcomes all to repentance — 'go, and sin no more' — not to remain unchanged. Welcome and the cross are inseparable.
roots_lines: English: a church welcome-statement, true as the gospel offer, corrupted into a banner of affirmation.
Gospel offer: 'whosoever will' (Rev. 22:17); 'him that cometh I will in no wise cast out' (John 6:37) — genuinely universal.
The threshold: 'Repent ye, and believe' (Mark 1:15) and the required wedding garment (Matt. 22:12) — welcome is to be made new, not to stay the same.
usage: 'All are welcome' is the most welcoming word ever spoken — and it welcomes you to repentance, not to your sin made comfortable.
Christ said 'neither do I condemn thee' and 'go, and sin no more' in one breath; keep both, or you have kept neither.
The door is open to every sinner; none may stay at the feast without the wedding garment of Christ's righteousness.

verdict.label: Examine
verdict.line: A true gospel welcome until it drops the call to repent — the open door that leads nowhere, the table without the cross.

etymology: Coined from The Fundamentals: A Testimony to the Truth (1910-1915), a twelve-volume set defending core Christian doctrines, and the 1920 use by editor Curtis Lee Laws for those who would 'do battle royal for the Fundamentals.' Originally an honorable self-designation; later a journalistic slur (especially after the 1925 Scopes Trial coverage) for any unsophisticated religious conservative.
biblical_def: In its root the word names a virtue: holding fast the fundamentals — the doctrines without which there is no Christianity. These are 'the faith which was once delivered unto the saints' (Jude 3): the inspiration and authority of Scripture, the deity and virgin birth of Christ, His substitutionary atonement, His bodily resurrection, His coming again. To be a fundamentalist in this original sense is simply to 'continue thou in the things which thou hast learned' (2 Tim. 3:14) and to refuse to surrender the foundations, 'for other foundation can no man lay than that is laid, which is Jesus Christ' (1 Cor. 3:11). The early Fundamentalists were largely faithful men contending against the modernist denial of these very doctrines (see theological-liberalism), and on the doctrines themselves they were right. The word's honorable core is the courage to say there are non-negotiables, and these are they.
webster_summary: Originally those who held and contended for 'the fundamentals' of the faith (the 1910s Fundamentals); now a slur for any firm conservative; reclaim the doctrinal core, concede the subculture's real excesses honestly.
webster_full: FUNDAMENTALIST, noun. Originally, one who affirms and contends for the fundamental doctrines of Christianity.
Source: The Fundamentals (1910-1915); Curtis Lee Laws (1920), one who would 'do battle royal for the Fundamentals.'
The fundamentals: inspiration of Scripture; deity and virgin birth of Christ; substitutionary atonement; bodily resurrection; second coming.
Later a journalistic slur (post-1925 Scopes coverage) for any anti-intellectual, separatist, or unsophisticated religious conservative — a sense that flattens the honorable core.
scriptures: Jude 1:3

Beloved, when I gave all diligence to write unto you of the common salvation, it was needful for me to write unto you, and exhort you that ye should earnestly contend for the faith which was once delivered unto the saints.
1 Corinthians 3:11
For other foundation can no man lay than that is laid, which is Jesus Christ.
2 Timothy 3:14
But continue thou in the things which thou hast learned and hast been assured of, knowing of whom thou hast learned them;
Ephesians 2:20
And are built upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets, Jesus Christ himself being the chief corner stone;
1 Timothy 6:20
O Timothy, keep that which is committed to thy trust, avoiding profane and vain babblings, and oppositions of science falsely so called:
corruption_summary: An honorable term for those who hold the fundamentals of the faith is now a slur flung at any conservative who holds firm; reclaim the doctrinal core, while honestly conceding the subculture's real excesses.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is twofold, and honesty requires naming both halves. First, the world's misuse: 'fundamentalist' has become a sneer, a one-word dismissal that lumps the man who simply believes the virgin birth and the resurrection together with the violent zealot of any religion, so that holding the fundamentals of Christianity is made to sound like a personality disorder. By this slur, conviction itself is pathologized: to believe there are non-negotiable doctrines is treated as small-minded, and the contending Jude commanded (Jude 3) is recast as bigotry. The faithful should not flinch at the word; on the doctrines, the early Fundamentalists were right, and the slur is aimed at the doctrines.

Second, the subculture's real failings, which the Reformed reader must concede without flinching. Twentieth-century fundamentalism, especially in its separatist and revivalist American forms, did accumulate genuine excesses: an anti-intellectualism that scorned learning (against 'the noble Bereans,' Acts 17:11); a legalism that bound consciences with extra-biblical rules (against Col. 2:20-23); a second- and third-degree separation that fractured fellowship over trifles; at times a harshness and a cult of personality far from the gentleness of Christ. These are not the world's slander; they are sins to be repented, and the dictionary names them honestly. To defend the doctrinal core is not to defend every fault of the movement that carried it.

The recovery distinguishes the foundation from the faults. There are fundamentals — 'other foundation can no man lay than that is laid, which is Jesus Christ' (1 Cor. 3:11) — and to hold them firmly is faithfulness, not fanaticism. But the manner of holding them must be the manner of Christ: firm in doctrine, humble in spirit, learned rather than obscurantist, gracious rather than censorious. The Reformed confessionalist keeps the fundamentals the original Fundamentalists kept, while leaving behind the cultural excesses they too often added to them.
roots_summary: From The Fundamentals (1910-1915), an honorable term for holding the faith's non-negotiables, now a slur for any firm conservative; reclaim the doctrinal core and repent the subculture's real excesses.
roots_lines: English: from The Fundamentals (1910-1915); Curtis Lee Laws (1920), 'battle royal for the Fundamentals.'
The core: the faith 'once delivered' (Jude 3) — Scripture, Christ's deity and virgin birth, atonement, resurrection, return.
The honest concession: the movement's later anti-intellectualism and legalism (cf. Acts 17:11; Col. 2:20-23) are faults to repent, not the doctrines to defend.
usage: They use 'fundamentalist' to pathologize conviction itself, as if believing the resurrection were a character flaw rather than the gospel.
On the fundamentals the early Fundamentalists were right; the slur is aimed past the men at the doctrines they held.
Keep the foundation and leave the faults: firm in doctrine, humble in spirit, learned rather than obscurantist.

verdict.label: Examine
verdict.line: Honorable in its doctrinal core, but the subculture's real excesses are faults to repent, not the foundation to defend.

etymology: A modern evangelical coinage joining heart (the biblical seat of mind, will, and affections) with posture (a bodily stance, used figuratively for an inward disposition). 'Heart posture' names the inward attitude or bearing of the soul toward God or others — a soft, contemporary churchy phrase for an old biblical reality.
biblical_def: The reality behind the phrase is thoroughly biblical: God weighs the disposition of the heart, not merely the outward act. 'The LORD seeth not as man seeth; for man looketh on the outward appearance, but the LORD looketh on the heart' (1 Sam. 16:7). He requires the inward bearing as well as the outward deed: 'this people draw near me with their mouth, and with their lips do honour me, but have removed their heart far from me' (Isa. 29:13). The heart is to be set, bowed, prepared: 'Ezra had prepared his heart to seek the law of the LORD' (Ezra 7:10); 'create in me a clean heart, O God; and renew a right spirit within me' (Ps. 51:10); 'My son, give me thine heart' (Prov. 23:26). 'Heart posture,' rightly meant, names this inward stance — the bowed, humble, God-ward disposition that must underlie all true obedience. The substance is sound; only the phrase is modern.
webster_summary: A soft modern churchy phrase for the disposition of the heart; basically sound (God weighs the heart, 1 Sam. 16:7) but often vague and used to spiritualize feelings over obedience.
webster_full: HEART POSTURE, noun phrase. The inward attitude, disposition, or bearing of the soul toward God or others.
A modern evangelical coinage: heart (the biblical seat of mind, will, and affections) + posture (figurative inward stance).
Sound in substance: God looks on the heart (1 Sam. 16:7) and requires the inward disposition, not lip-service only (Isa. 29:13).
Cautioned in use: often vague, and sometimes deployed to elevate how one feels above what one is commanded to do.
scriptures: 1 Samuel 16:7

But the LORD said unto Samuel, Look not on his countenance, or on the height of his stature; because I have refused him: for the LORD seeth not as man seeth; for man looketh on the outward appearance, but the LORD looketh on the heart.
Proverbs 4:23
Keep thy heart with all diligence; for out of it are the issues of life.
Psalm 51:10
Create in me a clean heart, O God; and renew a right spirit within me.
Isaiah 29:13

Wherefore the Lord said, Forasmuch as this people draw near me with their mouth, and with their lips do honour me, but have removed their heart far from me, and their fear toward me is taught by the precept of men:
Proverbs 23:26
My son, give me thine heart, and let thine eyes observe my ways.
corruption_summary: Basically a sound notion — God weighs the heart — but the soft phrase is often vague, and is sometimes used to spiritualize feelings and disposition over actual obedience.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition; the danger is subtler — a sound idea worn smooth by overuse and occasionally bent to excuse disobedience. 'Heart posture' rightly names what 1 Samuel 16:7 and Isaiah 29:13 establish: God is not content with the outward act but searches the inward disposition. So far it is wholesome. The first caution is mere vagueness: the phrase can become a pious filler, a way to sound spiritual ('I just want to check my heart posture') without the precision Scripture brings, which speaks of a clean heart, a contrite heart, a heart that keeps the commandments (Ps. 51:10, 17; John 14:15).

The graver misuse is to let inward 'posture' substitute for outward obedience — to treat having warm feelings toward God as if it were the same as doing what He says. Scripture binds the two: 'My son, give me thine heart, and let thine eyes observe my ways' (Prov. 23:26) — the given heart and the watched ways together. Christ rebukes the man who says 'Lord, Lord' with feeling but 'doeth not the things which I say' (Luke 6:46). A good 'heart posture' that does not issue in obedience is not the contrite heart God accepts but the lip-honour He rejects (Isa. 29:13). The phrase is safe only when the heart it describes is the heart that obeys.

The recovery is to keep heart and act welded as Scripture welds them. 'Keep thy heart with all diligence; for out of it are the issues of life' (Prov. 4:23) — the heart is guarded precisely because it issues in life and conduct. A right inward disposition is not an alternative to obedience but its spring; the bowed heart bows the body too. So the phrase may be kept, provided it is anchored: 'heart posture' means the God-ward, humble, repentant disposition that produces obedience — never a feeling that excuses its absence.
roots_summary: A modern phrase for the heart's disposition; sound in substance (God looks on the heart, 1 Sam. 16:7) but to be kept precise and welded to obedience, never a feeling that excuses it.
roots_lines: English: heart (biblical seat of mind, will, affections) + posture (figurative inward stance) — a modern evangelical coinage.
Hebrew: the biblical leb / lebab, the whole inner man — what 1 Sam. 16:7 says the LORD beholds.
Biblical weld: Prov. 23:26 binds the given heart to the watched ways — disposition and obedience together, never apart.
usage: He spoke much of his 'heart posture' and little of his obedience, but the LORD who looks on the heart also said, 'keep my commandments.'
A bowed heart bows the body too; right disposition is obedience's spring, not its substitute.
The phrase is safe when anchored: the God-ward, repentant heart that issues in doing what He says.

verdict.label: Neutral
verdict.line: A sound idea in a soft phrase — safe when it names the obeying heart, risky when it spiritualizes feeling over obedience.

etymology: An activist and therapeutic catchphrase of the 2010s-2020s ('do the work' of anti-racism, of 'deconstructing' one's biases, of 'unlearning' privilege). The definite article makes it a liturgy: there is a known, ongoing, never-finished 'Work' that the conscientious must perpetually perform to be justified before the movement.
biblical_def: Scripture sharply distinguishes two works: the finished work of Christ that saves, and the good works of the believer that flow from being saved. The first is complete and unrepeatable — on the cross the Lord cried, 'It is finished' (John 19:30); 'by one offering he hath perfected for ever them that are sanctified' (Heb. 10:14). Salvation is 'not of works, lest any man should boast' (Eph. 2:9), 'not by works of righteousness which we have done, but according to his mercy he saved us' (Titus 3:5). The second kind of work is real and required — believers are 'created in Christ Jesus unto good works' (Eph. 2:10) and must 'work out' their own salvation 'with fear and trembling' (Phil. 2:12) — but these are the fruit of justification, never its ground. The fatal question is always which Work justifies: Christ's finished Work, received by faith, or a Work of our own, perpetually demanded and never done.
webster_summary: An activist-liturgy phrase ('do the work' of anti-racism, etc.) smuggling a rival salvation-by-works into the church; but the Work that saves is finished — 'It is finished' (John 19:30).
webster_full: DOING THE WORK, slogan. An activist/therapeutic catchphrase for the ongoing, never-finished labor of anti-racism, bias-'unlearning,' or self-'deconstruction.'
The definite article ('the Work') marks it as a liturgy: a known, perpetual labor by which one is justified before the movement.
Structurally a rival soteriology: standing is achieved and maintained by one's own continual works, never finally complete.
Rebutted by the finished work of Christ (John 19:30; Heb. 10:14) and justification by grace through faith, not works (Eph. 2:8-9; Titus 3:5).
scriptures: John 19:30
When Jesus therefore had received the vinegar, he said, It is finished: and he bowed his head, and gave up the ghost.
Ephesians 2:8-9
For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God: Not of works, lest any man should boast.
Titus 3:5
Not by works of righteousness which we have done, but according to his mercy he saved us, by the washing of regeneration, and renewing of the Holy Ghost;
Hebrews 10:14
For by one offering he hath perfected for ever them that are sanctified.
Galatians 2:16

Knowing that a man is not justified by the works of the law, but by the faith of Jesus Christ, even we have believed in Jesus Christ, that we might be justified by the faith of Christ, and not by the works of the law: for by the works of the law shall no flesh be justified.
corruption_summary: An activist liturgy smuggles a rival salvation-by-works into the church: standing is earned by perpetually 'doing the Work,' a labor never finished — the exact opposite of the gospel, where the Work that saves is finished.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is soteriological at its root: 'the Work' is a counterfeit of justification. In the activist register, one is never righteous; one is only ever 'doing the work,' a labor of self-examination, confession of privilege, and ongoing penance that by design can never be completed — there is always more bias to 'unlearn,' more privilege to 'interrogate.' This is salvation by works in its purest form, and like every works-religion it offers no rest, only an endless ladder. Paul's verdict is total: 'by the works of the law shall no flesh be justified' (Gal. 2:16). A gospel that ends in 'it is finished' (John 19:30) and a liturgy whose whole genius is that the work is never finished are two different religions. # voice-lock-ok: progressive: the activist 'Work' is named here to rebut it.

When this framework enters the church, it does not merely add an extra duty; it displaces the cross. The believer's peace rests on a Work outside himself, 'perfected for ever' by 'one offering' (Heb. 10:14); the activist's standing rests on a work inside himself, never perfected, perpetually in arrears. To import 'doing the work' as the path to acceptance — before God or before the congregation — is to set the soul back under the law that condemns, to trade the finished righteousness of Christ for the unfinished righteousness of self. It is, structurally, the Galatian error: 'having begun in the Spirit, are ye now made perfect by the flesh?' (Gal. 3:3).

The recovery is the great distinction the Reformation recovered: the finished work of Christ for us, and the grateful good works of Christ in us, in that order and never reversed. We are 'created in Christ Jesus unto good works' (Eph. 2:10) — there is a real and lifelong labor of obedience, mortification, and love — but it is the fruit of a justification already complete, not the price of one still owed.
